$comment: Realisation for grc (docs/rules/grc.md): realise/engine runs zz, an invented language given whole, over the engine features grc needed (a rule's `strip`; accent rules by the notation's `prosody`: recessive, persistent, oxytone, ultima); realise/grc runs grc's own rules and lexicon (lexicons/grc), with `spellings: false` as the compiler's token check: one vector per branch of every rule, from a token of the course where one takes the branch (its note says which), else a course lexeme in a cell the course does not write (said in the note). rule:grc-no-comparative's one branch is never taken: it names a value (Degree=Sup) the language does not have, so that a comparative's cell of an adjective not comparable has no form.

vectors.note: A rule with `strip` takes the cited ending off and realises the citation cell too: the lemma is a realisation (ADR 0154), its boundary kept.
The ending -os goes and -ou takes its place; the accent stays on the stem (the persistent rule changes nothing, so it is no step).
The first ending of `strip` the form ends in goes, its accent with it: an oxytone's stem has none. ultima: the last syllable takes the accent, a circumflex where it is long (θεοῦ).
oxytone: a form with no accent takes an acute on its last syllable (θεοί).
A form with an accent is left as it is by the oxytone rule.
A form that ends in none of the rule's `strip` endings is not realised by the rule.

A listed stem is the stem: nothing is stripped. The persistent accent stays on its syllable as far as the last allows: four from the end is too far, and with a long last syllable it moves to the second from the end.
The rule of limitation: a long last syllable keeps an acute off the third syllable from the end (anthrópou).
A short last syllable leaves the accent on the third from the end: nothing changes, so the accent rule is no step.
A circumflex on the second syllable from the end becomes an acute before a long last syllable.
Before a short last syllable the accented long second syllable keeps its circumflex (the circumflex is a long vowel's).
Recessive: a short last syllable puts the acute on the third from the end, where the lemma had it: no change, no step.
The citation cell realised by a stripping rule: the long last syllable puts the acute on the second from the end.
A long second syllable before a short last takes the circumflex (λῦε).
The accent recedes onto the syllable before the limit, a preverb's last (περίμενε).
It goes no further back than that syllable, though a short last syllable would let it go to the third from the end (ἀπόδος, a listed stem).
A final -ai counts short (shortAtEnd): the acute stands three syllables from the end, on the diphthong's second letter; the lemma had it there, so no step.
